newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian parties decry talk of Abacha candidacy.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian parties decry talk of Abacha candidacy.

text.p: Nigeria's five political parties have expressed apprehension about speculation that military ruler General Sani Abacha may contest 1998 presidential elections aimed at restoring democracy by October of that year.
An official communique signed by leaders of the five parties on Tuesday urged Abacha to call rumour-peddlers to order.

"The parties noted with dismay and disquiet the tendency of certain political parties to associate the name and person of the head of state with their scheming by publicly declaring him as their presidential candidate, when the head of state has neither declared his membership of any party nor any ambition to contest for any elective office," they said in the statement.
It was issued after they met in the capital Abuja to review the transition to civil rule programme of Abacha following the postponement of local elections to March 1997 from the end of this month.
The postponement on Sunday raised doubts about the military's commitment to restoring full democracy by 1998, but the electoral commission said the target date remained in force.
The communique said the five political parties "re-affirmed their support for the programme."
But opposition leader Michael Ajasin said on Tuesday the postponement showed the military government had no genuine plan to restore democracy.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, plunged into crisis in June 1993 when the the previous military ruler annulled a presidential election to choose his successor.
Moshood Abiola, the undeclared winner of the annulled poll is in detention for proclaiming himself president and his supporters insist he should be freed and installed president.

"The easiest way out of the political imbroglio is to de-annul the 1993 presidential election and put in place a national government headed by Chief M.K.O. Abiola," Ajasin told reporters in his home in Owo, southwestern Nigeria.
